strengths: Introduces a large-scale (489K) multi-round visual CoT dataset spanning four diverse domains, substantially larger and more structurally rich (scene description + RoI + rationale per round) than prior visual-CoT resources such as Visual-CoT, CogCoM, and Chain-of-Spot.

The VisReason-Pro subset innovates by incorporating pseudo-3D cues (monocular depth + semantic segmentation) to generate depth-aware spatial relations (in front of/behind) combined with 2D relations, addressing a genuine gap in existing 2D-only visual-CoT datasets.

Comprehensive experimental validation: comparison against multiple strong open-source MLLM baselines on 11 source datasets, generalization tests on MME and V*Bench, RoI localization and 3D grounding evaluation on a newly proposed benchmark, ablation studies isolating the contribution of VisReason, VisReason-Pro, and the adaptive zoom-in strategy, plus a human/user study assessing answer accuracy, grounded faithfulness, and stepwise clarity.

Strong reproducibility support: the supplementary material provides detailed training configurations, full data-generation algorithms (pseudocode), all prompts used for generation/refinement/grading, and additional dataset/inference examples.

The adaptive 'zoom only when needed' design (skipping iterative cropping for large/easy targets) is a sensible efficiency-oriented choice that is empirically shown to preserve performance on easier domains (e.g., Doc/Text) while improving fine-grained and relational tasks.
weaknesses: The dataset's rationales, RoIs, and 3D-aware QA pairs are generated entirely by GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini with only an automatic 'verify-and-fix' routine (box adjustment to cover GT and area-ratio thresholds); there is no independent human verification of annotation quality/faithfulness at the dataset level, so the reliability and semantic correctness of the multi-round rationales themselves remain unvalidated at scale (the user study only evaluates final model outputs on 20 sampled items, not the underlying training annotations).

The '3D ground truth' used for depth-aware supervision and evaluation is itself pseudo-labeled from Depth-Anything V2 and Mask2Former/SAM2, not real depth sensors or human 3D annotations; consequently, the reported 3D-grounding metrics (e.g., absolute depth error) measure agreement with another model's pseudo-labels rather than true 3D accuracy, which is a circularity concern.

Evaluation on the main Visual-CoT benchmark relies on an LLM-based judge with a similarity-scoring rubric rather than exact-match or human-verified accuracy, which can introduce judge bias/inconsistency, especially since the paper's own models are trained on similarly LLM-generated rationale style.

Because VisReason and VisReason-Pro are built directly from the same source images/questions (Visual-CoT's regular and GQA portions) used for the benchmark, readers cannot easily verify there is no train/test leakage; the paper does not explicitly discuss dataset splitting/held-out guarantees in the main text.
The user study is small-scale (30 raters, only 20 sampled items per method), limiting statistical robustness of the qualitative claims about grounded faithfulness and stepwise clarity.

The method itself (SFT with LoRA on a fixed multi-round zoom-and-verify format) is technically straightforward and largely a natural extension of existing zoom-based visual CoT approaches (e.g., Chain-of-Focus, CogCoM, Visual-CoT); the core novelty lies primarily in dataset scale/domain breadth and depth augmentation rather than in new algorithmic or modeling contributions.

No comparison against recent RL-based 'thinking-with-images'/pixel-reasoning approaches (e.g., Pixel-Reasoner) as direct baselines, despite these being cited as closely related; only SFT-style baselines are compared quantitatively.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing visual-CoT resources are small, single-domain, or lack multi-round/depth-aware supervision, and VISREASON attempts to fill this gap at a large scale (489K + 165K examples) across four diverse domains (text/doc, fine-grained recognition, general VQA, spatial relation reasoning).
The data-generation pipeline is described in substantial detail (main paper + extensive supplementary material with algorithms and all prompts), which aids reproducibility.

Experiments are fairly comprehensive: comparison against multiple open-source MLLMs on an 11-dataset benchmark, an additional VISREASON-PRO benchmark for RoI localization and 3D grounding, external generalization tests (MME, V*Bench), ablations isolating dataset/zoom-in contributions, and a human study with three qualitative criteria.

The idea of coupling monocular depth and segmentation to synthesize 3D-aware spatial relations (in front of/behind combined with 2D relations) is a reasonable and relatively underexplored extension for visual CoT datasets.
weaknesses: The dataset's 'ground truth' is almost entirely synthesized by prompting GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini over existing images and object lists; there is no reported human verification rate, inter-annotator agreement, or systematic quality audit of the generated rationales, RoIs, or depth-based relations, despite the paper's framing of these as 'human-like' reasoning chains.

The VISREASON-PRO benchmark used for RoI/3D-grounding evaluation (Tab. 3, Tab. 4) is self-referential: the 'ground-truth' boxes and depth values used for scoring are themselves GPT/pipeline-generated (via GPT-4.1-mini + Depth-Anything V2 + Mask2Former pseudo-depth), not independently/manually annotated. This materially weakens the validity of the benchmark as an external evaluation of grounding quality, since models are effectively being scored against another model's outputs.

Final answer/accuracy evaluation on the main Visual-CoT benchmark relies exclusively on an LLM-based judge producing a continuous [0,1] score, without complementary exact-match/human-verified accuracy numbers for cross-checking; potential judge bias toward verbose CoT-style outputs (favoring the paper's own trained models) is not investigated or controlled for.

The reported improvements are modest in several settings: the fine-tuned models trail the un-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-2.5-7B backbone on several sub-tasks (DocVQA, TextCaps, TextVQA, SROIE, GQA, VSR) in Table 2, and the overall average gain (0.770→0.807) is relatively small given the scale of new supervision introduced; on MME, VISREASON-PRO-7B actually underperforms both the InternVL-2.5-8B baseline and VISREASON-7B.

Absolute grounding performance remains weak even for the proposed models (grounded ratio 0.276, IoU@0.75 of only 0.23), which somewhat undercuts claims of 'substantial improvements' in 3D grounding and interpretability.

The technical contribution beyond dataset curation is limited — training uses standard LoRA SFT on an existing backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) without new architectural or algorithmic innovation; the paper's framing of a 'unified training and inference pipeline' overstates the novelty of what is largely a standard fine-tuning recipe.

No explicit discussion of dataset limitations (e.g., propagated errors from monocular depth pseudo-labels, GPT hallucinations in rationales/boxes, or domain imbalance) or societal impact is provided in the main text, despite these being important given the synthetic nature of the annotations.

Depth-aware QA generation and evaluation both depend on the same imperfect monocular depth estimator (Depth-Anything V2), creating a risk of circularity where errors in depth estimation are baked into both the training labels and the evaluation ground truth, with no independent validation of depth accuracy against real 3D data.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing visual-CoT resources lack scale, multi-round stepwise supervision, and depth-aware grounding; the paper directly targets all three deficiencies.

Introduces a genuinely useful large-scale resource (489K VisReason + 165K VisReason-Pro) spanning four diverse domains (text/doc, fine-grained, general VQA, spatial relation reasoning), which should be broadly useful to the community for training and evaluating visual CoT models.

Novel incorporation of pseudo-3D cues (monocular depth + semantic segmentation) into the CoT generation pipeline to support ordinal depth reasoning alongside 2D spatial relations, an underexplored direction relative to prior 2D-only visual-CoT datasets.

Thorough experimental validation: results on the Visual-CoT benchmark, a newly constructed VisReason-Pro benchmark (RoI localization and 3D grounding metrics), external generalization benchmarks (MME, V*Bench), an ablation study isolating dataset/strategy contributions, and a human/user study — together forming a fairly comprehensive evidence package.

Strong reproducibility support: the paper provides extensive supplementary detail, including training hyperparameters, full data-generation algorithms (pseudocode), all prompts used for generation and grading, and additional qualitative examples.

Consistent and generally convincing empirical gains over strong open-source baselines (InternVL-2.5, LLaVA-NeXT, VisCoT, Qwen2.5-VL) on relation reasoning, fine-grained recognition, and general VQA, with corroborating human evaluation showing improved grounded faithfulness and stepwise clarity.
weaknesses: The dataset is built by expanding the existing Visual-CoT seed data (regular and GQA splits) using GPT-4.1-nano/mini generated rationales and RoIs with only heuristic (IoU-based) verify-and-fix correction; there is limited discussion of hallucination rates or systematic human quality auditing of the generated multi-round rationales beyond the small 20-item/30-rater user study.

The 3D grounding evaluation is partly circular: both the training annotations and the benchmark's pseudo-ground-truth depth/segmentation are derived from the same monocular depth (Depth-Anything V2) and segmentation (Mask2Former/SAM2) models used to build VisReason-Pro, so strong 3D-grounding scores may partly reflect alignment with the annotation pipeline's biases rather than true 3D understanding.

Absolute RoI localization accuracy remains modest (best IoU@0.5 = 0.34, IoU@0.75 = 0.23), suggesting that despite the multi-round supervision, precise spatial grounding is still far from reliable, which tempers claims about robust spatially grounded reasoning.

The proposed models underperform the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone on Text/Doc OCR-heavy tasks (e.g., DocVQA, TextVQA, SROIE), indicating that the added CoT supervision can trade off against baseline strengths in certain domains; this is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed or mitigated.

Evaluation on the main Visual-CoT benchmark relies on an LLM-based judge producing a scalar [0,1] score rather than exact-match or more standard task-specific accuracy metrics for many datasets, which introduces potential subjectivity/bias not fully addressed by calibration description alone.
No experiments at larger model scales or with other backbone families beyond Qwen2.5-VL-7B, limiting evidence that the dataset's benefits generalize across architectures/scales.

Limited discussion of licensing, potential biases inherited from source datasets (e.g., GQA, Open Images, Flickr30k), or societal/ethical considerations of releasing GPT-synthesized rationales at scale.

strengths: Large-scale dataset (489K examples + 165K high-fidelity VisReason-Pro subset) spanning four diverse domains, substantially larger and more richly annotated (multi-round RoI, rationales, depth cues) than prior visual-CoT resources such as Visual-CoT, CogCoM, VoCoT.
Thorough and transparent data-generation pipeline described in detail (main text and extensive supplementary algorithms/prompts), improving reproducibility.

Multiple forms of validation: a 2,200-example stratified human audit of annotation quality (answer consistency, RoI containment/tightness, rationale necessity/faithfulness) with Wilson confidence intervals, and a separate human calibration of the GPT-4o-mini automatic judge against human ratings.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental suite: fine-tuning on two backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B), ablations isolating VisReason vs. VisReason-Pro vs. adaptive zoom, RoI localization and depth-grounding metrics, external benchmark checks (MME, V*Bench), and a small user study.

Candid discussion of limitations, including pseudo-depth (not metric 3D) caveats, format-mismatch effects on Text/Doc tasks, and a clearly articulated 'cascading localization failure' vulnerability of the zoom-and-verify paradigm.
Useful diagnostic ablations (source-removal, direct-QA vs. multi-round CoT) that help contextualize where gains come from rather than overstating generality.
weaknesses: Gains are modest and domain-dependent: average improvement over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone is small (0.770→0.802), driven largely by two categories (CUB, OpenImages), while Doc/Text and some VQA/spatial subsets (e.g., DUDE, VSR, GQA) often regress under the default multi-round inference.

Second-backbone transfer (InternVL-2.5-8B) yields an overall weighted-average improvement of only +0.001, with several domains (Text/Doc, General VQA, GQA, VSR) decreasing after fine-tuning, undermining claims of consistent cross-backbone benefit.

The source-removal ablation shows that most fine-grained/spatial gains disappear when domain-matched training sources are excluded, suggesting the dataset's benefit is closer to in-domain specialization than to a generalizable reasoning skill, which somewhat tempers the 'human-like reasoning' framing in the abstract/intro.

Depth supervision is derived from noisy monocular depth estimation rather than any ground-truth 3D signal; while the paper appropriately caveats this, the practical value of the 'ordinal-depth' contribution for genuine spatial reasoning is not deeply validated beyond IoU/abs-diff metrics on the same noisy pseudo-labels used for training.

Evaluation relies heavily on an LLM-based judge (GPT-4o-mini); although calibrated against humans, agreement is moderate (Pearson r=0.758, exact agreement 73.3%), leaving some uncertainty in the reported score magnitudes, especially for small differences between methods.
The human user study is fairly small (30 raters, 20 items per method), limiting statistical power for the qualitative claims about answer accuracy, faithfulness, and clarity.

The core annotation pipeline is itself generated by GPT-4.1-series models rather than fully human-authored, so quality is bounded by the teacher model's own visual grounding and reasoning ability; the human audit checks consistency/tightness but does not fully assess whether the teacher's reasoning traces reflect genuinely correct causal justification versus post-hoc rationalization.

The 'cascading localization failure' limitation is significant: since the iterative zoom mechanism lacks a backtracking/zoom-out capability, an early RoI mistake can propagate, and no mitigation or quantitative frequency analysis of this failure mode is provided.

strengths: The dataset construction pipeline is comprehensive and well-documented, with multi-round RoI-grounded rationales, pseudo-depth/segmentation augmentation (Depth-Anything V2 + Mask2Former + SAM2), and detailed algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1-2) and prompts provided in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.

The paper reports an unusually thorough set of auxiliary studies for a dataset paper: a 2,200-example stratified human data-quality audit with Wilson CIs, human calibration of the GPT-4o-mini judge against human ratings, a 30-rater blinded user study, a second-backbone transfer experiment (InternVL-2.5-8B), and a source-removal ablation that honestly reports its own limitations (Sec. D.3).

The explicit comparison between multi-round CoT and direct-QA inference formats (Tab. 3, 7, 12) is a useful diagnostic that isolates protocol effects from capability changes, and the paper is unusually candid about failure modes such as cascading localization errors and the Doc/Text regression under multi-round inference.

Scale (489K + 165K examples) and four-domain coverage (text/doc, fine-grained, general VQA, spatial/depth relation) exceed several cited prior visual-CoT resources in raw size, and the explicit RoI + rationale + optional depth annotation format is a reasonable structured target for training zoom-and-verify behavior.
weaknesses: The primary evaluation benchmark ("Visual-CoT-Benchmark") is built from exactly the same source datasets (DocVQA, TextVQA, Flickr30k, GQA, VSR, Open Images, CUB, etc.) that constitute the training corpus, so the reported gains largely reflect in-domain/source-matched fine-tuning rather than demonstrated generalization of a reasoning "skill"; this is reinforced by the authors' own source-removal ablation (Tab. 14), which shows large performance drops when domain-relevant sources are excluded, undermining the paper's broader claims about cultivating generalizable human-like visual reasoning.

Core quantitative results rely entirely on a GPT-4o-mini LLM-as-judge scoring scheme rather than standard, directly comparable metrics (e.g., ANLS for DocVQA, EM/VQA-accuracy for TextVQA/GQA), making it difficult to situate the reported numbers against the broader literature; although a calibration study is provided, Pearson r=0.758 and 73.3% exact agreement with humans leave meaningful residual judge noise/bias that could affect the small (~0.03) average gains reported.

The data-generation annotator (GPT-4.1-Nano, and GPT-4.1-Mini for the "Pro" subset) is a comparatively weak/cheap model; using it to generate rationales, RoIs, and 3D-aware QA pairs for a dataset intended to teach "human-like" spatially grounded reasoning raises concerns about systematic rationale quality/faithfulness, especially in a domain (Text/Doc) where the audit itself documents the weakest rationale necessity/faithfulness scores (~71%) and where the model's own trained checkpoints show a performance drop versus the un-finetuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline.

Several headline results are mixed or negative: VisReason/VisReason-Pro fine-tuning decreases performance relative to the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone on most Doc/Text datasets (Tab. 2) and causes a substantial drop on the external V*Bench (0.791→0.603) and MME (0.861→0.777) under the model's native multi-round CoT inference mode — a benchmark specifically designed to test small-detail visual search, which should be the regime where this method shines; the paper's explanation ("format mismatch") is plausible but is essentially an admission that the proposed CoT training paradigm, as deployed, is not a strict improvement and requires format-switching logic to avoid regressions.

Novelty relative to prior multi-round/manipulation-based visual CoT work (CogCoM, VoCoT, Chain-of-Spot, Chain-of-Focus, VGR, Zebra-CoT) is primarily incremental: the core contribution is scaling up an existing dataset (Visual-CoT) with GPT-generated multi-round rationales plus monocular-depth/segmentation pseudo-3D augmentation, rather than a new modeling or data-curation mechanism; the depth signal itself is explicitly acknowledged as noisy ordinal pseudo-depth, not validated 3D ground truth, limiting the strength of the "depth-augmented spatial reasoning" claim.

Training uses relatively light LoRA (rank 32) adaptation on a strong pre-trained 7-8B backbone for only 1-2 epochs, so it is unclear how much of the reported behavior change is attributable to the dataset's distinctive content versus simply exposing the backbone to its own training-source test distributions in a new output format; a cleaner comparison against RL-based competitors (e.g., Chain-of-Focus with RL, Pixel-Reasoner) is largely absent (CoF is only compared in its SFT variant).

The cascading-localization-error vulnerability (acknowledged in Sec. 5.4) is a structural weakness of the proposed zoom-and-verify inference paradigm with no mitigation offered beyond flagging it as future work, which is a non-trivial reliability concern for a method whose central selling point is multi-step visual grounding.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing visual-CoT datasets are small, single-step, or lack spatial/depth grounding; VisReason provides large-scale (489K + 165K Pro) multi-round, RoI-grounded, depth-augmented process supervision across four diverse domains.

The data generation pipeline is well-engineered and clearly described (iterative zoom-and-verify with GT-coverage constraints, adaptive single-step shortcut for large objects, depth/segmentation-derived pseudo-3D cues via Depth-Anything V2 + Mask2Former + SAM2), and is fully documented with algorithms in the supplementary material for reproducibility.

Experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: results across two backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B), an ablation isolating VisReason vs. VisReason-Pro vs. adaptive zoom, a dedicated depth/RoI grounding benchmark, a 30-rater human study, and a large stratified human audit (2,200 examples) of annotation quality with Wilson confidence intervals.

The authors calibrate their automatic GPT-4o-mini judge against human ratings (Pearson/Spearman/QWK reported) and release the grading prompt/parser, strengthening reproducibility and trustworthiness of the reported numbers.

Commendable transparency about limitations: explicit discussion of the Text/Doc performance drop under multi-round CoT (diagnosed as protocol mismatch via a direct-QA control), cascading localization failure modes, noisy pseudo-depth (not metric 3D), and a conservative source-removal ablation showing that gains partly depend on domain-relevant training sources rather than claiming universal generalization.
weaknesses: The core contribution is largely a re-annotation/augmentation pipeline applied to existing source datasets (Visual-CoT/GQA, TextVQA, DocVQA, CUB, Flickr30k, etc.) rather than newly collected imagery or tasks; the paper should more clearly delineate what is genuinely new content versus repurposed data with GPT-generated rationales.

Overall accuracy gains on the main Visual-CoT benchmark are relatively modest in aggregate (0.770 → 0.802 average), with some domains (Text/Doc, VSR) showing decreases under the default multi-round format, partially offsetting the paper's stronger claims of 'substantial improvements.'

Second-backbone transfer results (InternVL-2.5-8B) are mixed: overall weighted average is essentially flat (0.738 → 0.740), with notable regressions on GQA (-0.140) and VSR (-0.095), suggesting the benefits are backbone- and calibration-dependent rather than robustly general.

The source-removal ablation (Table 14) shows large performance drops when domain-relevant sources (CUB, spatial-relation data) are excluded, indicating that reported gains are substantially attributable to matched training/test domains rather than broadly transferable reasoning skills — this tempers claims of cultivating general 'human-like' visual reasoning.

Automatic evaluation throughout the paper relies heavily on an LLM-based judge (GPT-4o-mini); while calibration is provided (exact agreement 73.3%, within-0.5 92.5%), this is still an approximate proxy and could introduce systematic biases not fully captured by the reported correlation statistics.

The 'zoom-and-verify' paradigm's cascading localization failure mode (no backtracking/self-correction) is acknowledged but not addressed with any mitigation or quantitative analysis of its frequency/impact, leaving it as an open concern rather than a resolved limitation.
